definition.text: Fisheries management is the set of tasks that guide users and managers toward the best use of renewable aquatic resources, mainly fish.

facts.text: Its goal is to produce lasting biological, environmental and socioeconomic benefits from renewable aquatic resources.
Wild fish stocks count as renewable when they produce a yearly surplus that careful management can harvest without lowering future productivity.
The FAO says there is no clear, generally accepted definition, and uses a working one covering information gathering, planning, decision-making, rule-making and enforcement.
Modern management is often a government system of rules based on set objectives, enforced through monitoring, control and surveillance.
Fisheries have been explicitly managed in some places for hundreds of years; Norway passed a law on the Lofoten fishery in 1816.
In Europe, government management to protect fish stocks began after the first Overfishing Conference in London in 1936.
A 2008 World Bank and FAO report put the economic loss from depleted stocks and poor management at US$50 billion a year.
Fisheries scientist Milo Adkison argues that the main limit on management decisions is the lack of good-quality data.

definition.text: In economics, the aim of fisheries management is to maximise the present value of all future profits from a fishery, which is treated as a common property resource.

facts.text: Economists often define fisheries as common property resources, which suffer the problems of open-access goods, chiefly overexploitation.
The problem was first analysed at length in H. Scott Gordon's 1954 article and Anthony D. Scott's 1955 article, both in the Journal of Political Economy.
Gordon showed that without intervention, fishers keep entering until total value minus costs is zero, so profits dissipate.
Both articles were foundational for environmental economics, giving the basic economic case for managing renewable resources.
A main remedy for this market failure is to assign property rights, which the broadest economic survey suggests prevents population collapse.
Newer models add differing technologies and costs among users, uncertainty and the biology of fish population growth.

definition.text: Fisheries regulation falls into four core categories that limit either what goes into fishing (inputs such as boats and gear) or what comes out (the catch), directly or indirectly.

facts.text: Indirect input control is vessel licensing; direct input control is limited entry.
Output controls are rules on catching techniques or equipment (indirect) and catch quotas with technical regulation (direct).
Technical measures include minimum mesh sizes, bans on certain nets or weapons, and limits on vessel numbers and time at sea.
Many countries run fisheries ministries that control fishing within their exclusive economic zones.

definition.text: Large, old female fish turn out to matter far more than young ones for keeping fisheries productive, contrary to traditional management.

facts.text: Traditional management thinned out old, slow-growing fish to leave room for younger, faster-growing ones.
Larvae from older mothers grow faster, resist starvation better and are much more likely to survive.
Ignoring older fish may help explain recent collapses of some major US West Coast fisheries; marine reserves let populations age naturally.

definition.text: Ecosystem-based fisheries management manages fishing for the health and productivity of the whole ecosystem rather than for single target species.

facts.text: Current scientific consensus favours it as the most workable way to balance human needs, keep ecosystem services and limit ecological harm.
Instead of focusing on one species, it is organised around ecosystem services.
A 2007 set of 'ten commandments' urged keeping big old females, natural stock boundaries, seafloor habitats and food-web links.
It also asks managers to adapt to climate change, account for fishing-driven evolution and include human social and economic systems.
Pitcher and Pauly argue that rebuilding ecosystems, not sustainability as such, should be the goal, since harvesting simplifies ecosystems toward small, low-level species.

definition.text: Ecopath with Ecosim is a software suite for modelling marine ecosystems, widely used in fisheries management.

facts.text: It began as a NOAA initiative and was later developed mainly at the University of British Columbia's Fisheries Centre.
In 2007 NOAA named it one of the ten biggest scientific breakthroughs in its 200-year history.
As of 2010 it had 6000 registered users in 155 countries.

definition.text: The BIDE model is the basic accounting rule of population dynamics: next period's numbers equal current numbers plus births and immigrants, minus deaths and emigrants.

facts.text: It is written N1 = N0 + B − D + I − E.
In wild fisheries, immigration and emigration happen but are usually not measured.
Over-simple models that ignored fish size, age, bycatch and habitat damage have sped the collapse of key stocks.

definition.text: A sustainable fishery is conventionally one harvested at a rate at which the fish population does not decline over time because of fishing.

facts.text: It combines theory such as population dynamics with practice: quotas, curbing illegal fishing, protected areas and certification.
Worries include lost yield, stocks losing diversity and resilience, boom-and-bust cycles and fishing down marine food webs.
Global wild fisheries are believed to have peaked and begun to decline.
Fisheries and aquaculture support the livelihoods of over 500 million people, mostly in developing countries.
Over 70% of fish species are fully exploited, overexploited, depleted or recovering from depletion.
A 2021 UN report said sustainable fisheries made up about 0.1 per cent of global GDP in 2017.

definition.text: There are three ways to define a sustainable fishery: long-term constant yield, preserving intergenerational equity, and maintaining a whole biological, social and economic system.

facts.text: Constant yield is called naive because marine stocks fluctuate naturally.
The widely accepted intergenerational view counts only damage needing more than one generation to rebuild as unsustainable.
The system view may accept losing some species if the ecosystem keeps its integrity and keeps delivering useful products.

definition.text: Overfishing in the traditional sense, catching so much that yield falls below what lighter fishing would give, is not automatically unsustainable.

facts.text: A salmon run kept at half its optimal spawning escapement can be fished indefinitely at lower yield.
Hilborn calls such overfishing a misallocation of society's resources rather than a conservation threat, but it can precede collapse.
Hilborn says persisting with fishing while stocks collapse is largely a product of institutional failure.

definition.text: Repeatedly dragging heavy bottom trawls and dredges over the seabed flattens its habitats and radically changes the communities living there.

facts.text: Nearly all continental shelves and large areas of slopes, ridges and seamounts have been trawled repeatedly.
For fifty years governments and bodies such as the Asian Development Bank encouraged building trawler fleets.
Mangrove loss of about 0.5 percent a year since the 2000s shrinks nursery habitat that over four million mangrove fishers rely on.

definition.text: In 1883 Thomas Huxley claimed overfishing was scientifically impossible and the great sea fisheries inexhaustible, even as fisheries were already collapsing.

facts.text: By then the Atlantic halibut fishery had already collapsed and never recovered.
The United States Fish Commission had been set up 12 years earlier to find out why New England fisheries were declining.

definition.text: Maximum sustainable yield (MSY) is, in theory, the largest catch that can be taken from a stock year after year for an indefinite period.

facts.text: MSY keeps a population at the size where it grows fastest, harvesting the individuals that would otherwise be added to it.
Small populations grow slowly because few fish breed; near carrying capacity crowding stops growth; in between, at half carrying capacity in the logistic model, the surplus is largest.
Modern fisheries models refine this, putting MSY at around 30% of the unexploited population size.
MSY is usually higher than the optimum sustainable yield and the maximum economic yield.
It became popular in the 1950s and was adopted as the main goal by bodies such as the IWC and ICCAT.
A 1955 international MSY treaty let foreign fleets fish off any coast unless the coastal nation proved its fish were overfished.
MSY was written into the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea even as scientists questioned it.

definition.text: The simplest harvest model subtracts a constant catch H from logistic population growth and finds where catch equals growth.

facts.text: The population is at equilibrium when it stops growing, that is when dN/dt = 0 and growth equals harvest.
With logistic growth the maximum harvest equals one-fourth of carrying capacity K times the intrinsic growth rate r, reached at half of K.
Below MSY there are two equilibria: the higher is stable, the lower collapses toward extinction after any shock.
The MSY point itself is semi-stable, a knife-edge where a small fall in numbers spirals to extinction unless catch is cut.
Harvesting a fixed percentage or a constant effort instead of a fixed number avoids some of these instabilities.
Any harvest pulls a population below its original carrying capacity; sustainable harvest is possible only because of density dependence.

title: Criticism of maximum sustainable yield
article: Maximum sustainable yield#Limitations of MSY approach

definition.text: Maximum sustainable yield, though widely used by agencies managing fish, forests and wildlife, has been heavily criticised by ecologists on theoretical and practical grounds.

facts.text: In 1977 Peter Larkin argued it risked populations, ignored spatial variation and other species, counted benefits but not costs, and bent to political pressure.
Estimates suffer from poor model assumptions, unreliable data and treating all fish as identical regardless of age or size.
A fixed yearly MSY catch ignores natural swings in abundance and usually depletes stocks, so scientists now speak of maximum average yield.
Early New Zealand orange roughy quotas assumed fast breeding, but the fish turned out long-lived and slow, and stocks were depleted.
Many conservation biologists regard MSY as dangerous and misused, and it is blamed for collapses of many fisheries.

contested_note: Agencies still use MSY widely while many ecologists and conservation biologists consider it dangerous.

definition.text: Fisheries science is the academic discipline of understanding and managing fisheries.

facts.text: It draws on oceanography, marine and freshwater biology, ecology, population dynamics, economics, statistics and decision analysis.
New fields have grown out of it, such as bioeconomics and fisheries law.
Research uses specialised vessels that tow nets, sample plankton and water, and carry acoustic fish-finders.
Fedor Baranov's 1918 catch equation is perhaps the most used equation in fisheries modelling.
Michael Graham's 'Great Law of Fishing' holds that unlimited fisheries become unprofitable.

definition.text: The Gordon-Schaefer model is a bioeconomic model of a fishery that combines fish population growth with the costs and revenues of fishing.

facts.text: It accounts for biological growth rates, carrying capacity, and total and marginal costs and revenues, and can compute maximum sustainable yield.
It compares three scenarios: a monopoly owner, the biological optimum of MSY, and open access.
A profit-maximising owner fishes until marginal revenue equals marginal cost; monopolies produce less at higher prices than competitive markets.
Under open access, each year's catch is set by demand and costs, ignoring effects on future years.
Gordon's 1954 analysis showed that under open access entry continues until total value minus costs is zero.

title: Individual fishing quota

definition.text: Individual fishing quotas, also called individual transferable quotas, are catch shares: a regulator sets a total allowable catch and hands portions of it to individual fishers.

facts.text: The total allowable catch is set per species, usually by weight and for a given period.
Quotas can usually be bought, sold and leased, a feature called transferability.
As of 2008, 148 major fisheries had adopted some form of the approach, and about 10% of the marine harvest was managed by ITQs.
The Netherlands, Iceland and Canada adopted them first in the late 1970s; New Zealand made ITQs national policy in 1986.
Like pollution quotas, ITQs are a cap-and-trade approach, but they regulate the industry's actual product rather than a by-product.
A 2008 study of 11,000 fisheries found catch share fisheries only half as likely to fail as open-access ones, nearly a third of which had collapsed.
Compared with other modern management schemes, however, IFQ fisheries show no long-term ecological advantage.
Alaska's halibut season, cut to two or three days before ITQs in 1995, now lasts nearly eight months.

contested_note: Studies disagree on whether IFQs improve stock health, and critics fault their social effects on small-scale fishers.

title: Rule of capture
article: Individual fishing quota#A move to privatisation and market-based mechanisms

definition.text: The rule of capture means a fisher owns a fish only once it is caught, which economists see as the main driver of overfishing.

facts.text: It encourages competitive racing and over-investment in boats and gear.
Without a long-term right to the stock, no one has a reason to conserve fish for the future.
Each boat plays a zero-sum game: any fish it leaves will likely be taken by another boat.

definition.text: The race to fish is the scramble to catch as much as possible during short open seasons, which catch shares are designed to end.

facts.text: Early management set a fishing season whose length tracked how abundant the stock was.
With catch shares, fishers can schedule trips as they like, boom-and-bust market cycles fade, and fishing in hazardous weather becomes unnecessary.
Under a total allowable catch each boat competes to land fish before the quota is reached, which pushes owners toward overcapitalization.
In Alaskan halibut the race cut the season to one 24-hour dash; the resource-economics text says ITQs later ended overcapitalization and spread the catch over time.

sources.title: 6.3: Case Study- Marine Fisheries - Engineering LibreTexts (Environmental and Resource Economics (Cabezas))

title: Quota allocation: grants versus auctions

definition.text: Fishing quotas can first be handed out free, usually by past catch, or sold at auction, and the choice decides who captures the resource's value.

facts.text: Grants by catch history give individuals a valuable right at no cost and are inherently political.
Auctions repay the public for access, like US radio spectrum auctions that raised tens of billions of dollars.
Russia's 2019 crab quota auction raised about 2 billion euro.
In Iceland critics argue quotas should be returned to the state and auctioned so the public gets a fair share of profits.

contested_note: Whether quotas should be granted to incumbents or auctioned is a live political dispute, notably in Iceland.

title: Criticisms of individual fishing quotas

definition.text: Critics say individual fishing quotas privatise a public resource, concentrate it in few hands and hurt fishing communities.

facts.text: First recipients get windfall profits, while later entrants must buy or lease the right to fish.
About eight companies control 80% of New Zealand's fisheries through quota purchases.
Bering Sea crab lease fees can reach 80% of landed value, leaving active fishers 20% of revenue.
Leasing gives rise to 'armchair fishermen' who hold quota but do not fish.

contested_note: Supporters credit IFQs with preventing collapses; critics stress consolidation, job loss and harm to coastal communities.

definition.text: Highgrading is catching more fish than a quota allows and dumping the less valuable ones so that the quota is filled with the best fish.

facts.text: Many dumped fish are already dead or die soon, adding to the drain on stocks.
ITQs can change the criteria fishers use to decide which fish to keep.

definition.text: A marine protected area (MPA) is a protected part of the seas, oceans or estuaries where human activity is restricted for conservation.

facts.text: Rules vary widely, covering development, fishing methods, seasons, catch limits and bans on disturbing marine life.
Not all MPAs are no-take zones: less than 1 percent of US waters are no-take.
Meta-analyses show no-take reserves give the biggest ecological benefits, largest when well-monitored, over ten years old and suitably sized.
Biodiversity in fully protected MPAs rose by an average of 23% after designation.
MPAs can support fishing through stock recovery and create jobs through ecotourism; a 2024 meta-analysis found no net cost to fisheries across 24 countries.
In 2020 only about 7.5 to 8% of the global ocean was under a conservation designation.
Some MPAs are criticised by indigenous peoples for impinging on their land-use rights.

definition.text: Spillover is the net movement of fish, eggs and larvae from a recovering marine protected area into the fishing grounds around it.

facts.text: A 2020 meta-analysis of 23 fully protected areas found commercial species up to 80% more abundant inside, and biomass 54% higher near boundaries than farther away.
It sustains fishing nearby without extracting anything inside the reserve; such benefits are well documented worldwide.
Coastal MPAs are increasingly recognised by scientists and small-scale fishers as raising the density and size of commercial species in local waters.

title: Displaced fishing effort

definition.text: Displaced fishing effort is the worry that closing an area to fishing just pushes the same fishing elsewhere, cancelling the reserve's benefits.

facts.text: Studies accounting for displacement suggest MPAs can still yield a net biodiversity gain when sensitive species are present.
Displacement can still raise costs for fishers.

contested_note: Fisheries scientists dispute whether no-take MPAs benefit biodiversity once displaced effort is counted.

definition.text: Overfishing is taking fish from a body of water faster than the species can naturally replace itself, so its numbers there keep falling.

facts.text: It can happen in any water body, from ponds and rivers to oceans, and leads to depletion, slower growth and low biomass.
Sustained overfishing can cause critical depensation, where a population can no longer sustain itself and is wiped out locally or globally.
The share of stocks within biologically sustainable levels fell from 90% in 1974 to 66.9% in 2015.
FAO reported that in 2017, 34 percent of marine fish stocks were overfished.
Collapsed stocks may not return: after trout are overfished, carp can take over and stop trout re-establishing.
Overfishing has reduced fish and marine mammal biomass by 60% since the 1800s.
Illegal catch is estimated at 11 to 26 million tonnes, 14–33% of the world's reported catch.
Remedies include regulation, removing subsidies, gentler fishing gear, aquaculture and consumer awareness.

definition.text: Biologists recognise three types of overfishing: growth overfishing, recruitment overfishing and ecosystem overfishing.

facts.text: Growth overfishing catches fish smaller, on average, than the size that gives the most yield per recruit, so total yield is lower.
Recruitment overfishing depletes the spawning adults until too few remain to replenish the stock.
Recruitment overfishing is treated with moratoriums, quotas and minimum size limits to rebuild spawning biomass.
Ecosystem overfishing shifts the ecosystem toward small forage species as large predators decline.

definition.text: Biological overfishing is fishing so hard that the stock's growth slows; economic overfishing is catching more than the maximum economic yield, where resource rent is highest.

facts.text: Whether there is overfishing depends on what counts as an acceptable level of fishing.
Economic overfishing adds the cost of fishing to the judgement, making the fishery less profitable than it could be.
A dynamic version uses a discount rate to maximise the present value of resource rent over all future catches.

definition.text: A harvest control rule is a set of pre-agreed tools that ties how much may be caught to the estimated state of the stock.

facts.text: Constant catch and constant fishing mortality are two simple types.
Major fisheries worldwide now use harvest control rules with a precautionary approach.
The traffic-light convention sets rules around critical values that are adjusted as more is learned.

definition.text: Fishing capacity is the most a fishery's boats and gear could catch, measured either by the capital fully used (input) or by the maximum catch (output).

facts.text: Output capacity assumes inputs fully used given the stock's biomass and age structure and current technology.
Capacity utilisation compares a fleet's actual catch or inputs with its capacity.
A World Bank and FAO report said half the world's fishing fleet could be scrapped with no change in catch.

definition.text: In an open-access fishery, competition drives fishers to invest until their costs equal their revenue, so the resource rent is wiped out.

facts.text: Because no one can be excluded, a fisher who wants a bigger catch takes it from someone else's share.
Gordon showed that overexploitation and rent dissipation arise in open-access fisheries, rooted in the property rights regime.
Fish move across jurisdictions, so one country's conservation can be exploited by another.
The industry's financial stake leads to lobbying that can block or weaken anti-overfishing policy.
The tragedy of the commons can create perverse incentives for more fisheries subsidies.

definition.text: A fishery is either the business of catching or raising fish and other aquatic life or, more often, the place where this happens, the fishing grounds.

facts.text: The FAO defines a fishery as an activity leading to harvesting fish, whether wild-caught or farmed.
A fishery is usually defined by its people, species, area, fishing method, class of boats and purpose.
In fisheries, 'fish' is a collective term that includes molluscs, crustaceans and any aquatic animal harvested for economic value.
About 500 million people worldwide depend economically on fisheries.
Close to 90% of catches come from oceans and seas; most marine fisheries lie near coasts where nutrients make fish abundant.
Fisheries were once 'first-come, first-served', but overfishing has forced more regulation.
Total fish production hit a record 171 million tonnes in 2016, 88% of it eaten directly by people.
A 2014 estimate put fisheries' contribution at US$270 billion a year to global GDP, with up to US$50 billion more possible from fully sustainable fishing.

definition.text: Fisheries are divided into commercial, recreational and subsistence sectors, and can be saltwater or freshwater, wild or farmed.

facts.text: Capture fisheries are broadly industrial, small-scale or artisanal, and recreational.
About 85% of marine fisheries production is finfish, mainly anchoveta, Alaska pollock and skipjack tuna.
Reduction fisheries, which process catch into products, are distinguished from others.

definition.text: Climate change affects fisheries through warming, acidifying and oxygen-poor oceans, and through altered temperatures, flows and habitats in fresh waters.

facts.text: It is shifting where fish live and how productive species are, changing the availability and trade of fish products.
The biggest falls in maximum catch potential are expected in the tropics, mostly in the South Pacific.
Global ocean catch is expected to fall 6 percent by 2100, and 11 percent in tropical zones.
Acidification makes it harder for shellfish, corals and zooplankton to build shells, putting 'cracks in the food chain'.
Overfished stocks, smaller and less genetically diverse, are more sensitive to climate stress.
Fish provides essential nutrition to 3 billion people, and poor, rural fishing communities are most exposed.
Fishing vessels caused about 0.5 percent of global CO2 emissions in 2012, 172.3 million tonnes.
Cutting fleet overcapacity and rebuilding stocks could raise resilience and returns by US$50 billion a year; removing fuel subsidies cuts both emissions and overfishing.

definition.text: Fisheries law is an emerging specialist field of law that studies fisheries management approaches such as catch shares and territorial use rights.

facts.text: It also covers international treaties, seafood safety, aquaculture and feed regulation, and access to justice for small-scale and aboriginal fishers.
The field is rarely taught at law schools, leaving a gap in advocacy and research.
The 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, in force from 1994, was one of the first such international laws.

title: Territorial use rights for fishing
article: Fisheries law#Territorial Use Rights for Fishing (TURF)

definition.text: Territorial use rights for fishing (TURFs) give communities or individuals exclusive fishing privileges over a defined area to prevent overexploitation.

facts.text: They usually go to communities with long traditions of sustainable fishing and are run by local fishers, with government-set conservation rules.
The most successful examples are in Chile and Japan; Chile has over 700 TURFs covering around 1100 square kilometres.
Because fishers depend on their own areas, they have an incentive to manage them sustainably.
Chile's TURFs for artisanal fisheries helped rebuild seabed fish stocks and raised fishers' compliance.

definition.text: Aquaculture, or aquafarming, is the controlled farming of aquatic organisms such as fish, crustaceans, molluscs, algae and aquatic plants.

facts.text: It raises freshwater, brackish and saltwater populations under controlled conditions, unlike commercial fishing, which harvests wild fish.
Stagnant wild harvests and growing demand for protein pushed farmers to domesticate more marine species, raising hopes of a 'Blue Revolution'.
With capture production static since the late 1980s, aquaculture has supplied the continuing growth in fish for human consumption.
In 2016 aquaculture made up 47 percent of the 171 million tonnes of fish produced, and in 2014 farmed fish overtook wild fish as human food.
Farming carnivorous fish like salmon does not relieve wild stocks because they are fed fishmeal and fish oil from wild forage fish.
Shrimp farming helped destroy about 20 percent of mangrove forests since 1980, and a 200,000-salmon farm discharges more faecal waste than a city of 60,000.
Shellfish farming adds filter-feeding capacity that can significantly improve water quality.
Farming creates private stocks, giving farmers a reason to conserve them.

definition.text: Integrated multi-trophic aquaculture recycles the wastes of one farmed species as food or fertiliser for another.

facts.text: Fed species such as fish or shrimp are combined with extractive species such as shellfish to balance the system environmentally and economically.
Bivalves like oysters and mussels feed on the surrounding natural production rather than added feed, so shellfish farming is usually seen as benign.

definition.text: The Beverton–Holt model is a classic discrete-time population model that predicts next generation's numbers from this generation's, levelling off at carrying capacity.

facts.text: Ray Beverton and Sidney Holt introduced it for fisheries in 1957.
Their 1957 work on North Sea fisheries became the theoretical basis of North European management in the 1960s.
It is the discrete-time counterpart of the logistic growth equation, and can be solved exactly.
The Ricker model generalises it to include scramble competition.

definition.text: Bycatch is fish or other marine life caught unintentionally while fishing for particular species or sizes.

facts.text: It may be the wrong species, the wrong sex, or undersized young of the target species.
Bycatch is about a quarter of all marine catch and is usually thrown back to die.
Shrimp trawls take two percent of the world's catch by weight but produce over one-third of all bycatch.
Gillnets, longlines and bottom trawls cause most bycatch, which includes dolphins, sea turtles and seabirds.
An estimated 100,000 albatross a year are killed on longlines.
Remedies include closing areas with high bycatch and changing fishing gear.
Norway's 'no discards' policy makes fishers keep everything they catch.

definition.text: Bycatch reduction devices and other gear changes let unwanted animals escape from fishing gear.

facts.text: Turtle excluder devices use a grid that deflects turtles out of a trawl net through an opening.
Approved US devices cut finfish bycatch by 30%, though surveys suggest they work less well than thought.
Designing gear to be more selective is called conservation engineering; bigger mesh openings let small fish escape.
Streamer lines cut seabird deaths in Alaskan longline fisheries by about 70%.

definition.text: Catch per unit effort (CPUE) is an indirect measure of how abundant a target species is, based on how much is caught for a given amount of fishing.

facts.text: A falling CPUE signals overexploitation, while a steady CPUE signals sustainable harvesting.
It does not disrupt normal harvesting and is easy to collect and analyse, so harvesters themselves can use it.
The main difficulty is defining the unit of effort, and CPUE is often not linearly related to abundance.

definition.text: Density dependence is when a population's growth rate is controlled by how crowded the population is.

facts.text: In negative density dependence, crowding, predators and competition slow growth; each individual leaves fewer offspring.
In positive density dependence, or the Allee effect, growth speeds up as density rises.
Fish populations can be harvested sustainably because thinning them out raises growth, the density-dependent response.

definition.text: Discards are the part of a catch that is not kept on board but thrown back into the sea, often dead or dying.

facts.text: Fish are discarded for economic and political reasons: they are unmarketable, below minimum landing size, or over quota.
Discards are part of bycatch; highgrading, dumping marketable fish to make room for more valuable ones, also causes them.
North Sea discards were estimated at 800,000–950,000 tonnes a year, about one-third of the weight landed.
Survival varies by species and gear, from 88 to 98 per cent for some flatfish and sharks to much lower for roundfish.

definition.text: A discard ban requires fishers to land what they catch, so that dead discards are counted in the fishing mortality used for management.

facts.text: Norway banned discarding some commercial species in 1987, combined with monitoring and closing areas when bycatch gets too high.
In New Zealand, discarding rose right after ITQs began, until the government raised payment for over-quota landings from 10 to 50 per cent of market price.
Older EU quota rules forced fishers to discard over-quota fish; the reformed Common Fisheries Policy added a Landing Obligation.

title: Exclusive economic zone

definition.text: An exclusive economic zone (EEZ) is a sea area, set by the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, where a coastal state has exclusive rights to explore and use marine resources.

facts.text: It runs from the edge of territorial waters at 12 nautical miles to 200 nautical miles from the coast.
Territorial waters once extended only 3 nautical miles, the range of a cannon shot.
EEZ boundaries are a common source of conflict; the UK–Iceland Cod Wars ended with a 1976 agreement.
Fish stocks that cross EEZ boundaries, transboundary stocks, are a key concept in controlling them.
Beyond EEZs fishing is hard to control, and most high-seas fisheries survive only on subsidies.
About one-third of the ocean lies within EEZs.
It stretches from 12 to 200 nautical miles from the coast.
EEZs were introduced to end heated clashes over fishing rights, as oil also grew important.

notes: Also drafted in biodiversity-agreements-and-targets; fold at merge.

sources.title: United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea
sources.key: United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea

definition.text: Fish mortality is a measure used in fisheries population models for the loss of fish from a stock through death.

facts.text: Natural mortality (M) covers deaths unrelated to fishing, such as disease, predation, old age or pollution; fishing mortality (F) covers deaths from fishing gear.
The two rates add up to total mortality: Z = M + F, usually calculated per year.
Fishing mortality can be estimated by dividing the catch, including landings and dead discards, by the mean stock size.
Comparing deaths with births or recruits shows whether a population is growing or shrinking, which helps managers set harvest limits.

definition.text: A fish stock is a subpopulation of one fish species whose growth, recruitment and deaths, including from fishing, are treated as the main drivers of its numbers.

facts.text: Fish tend to form partly separate populations that breed mostly among themselves, so fishing one population may not affect its neighbour.
Fisheries science defines a stock as a semi-discrete group of fish with definable attributes of interest to managers.
The FAO found that stocks fished within biologically sustainable levels fell from 90% in 1974 to 62.3% in 2021.
A 2020 FAO report classed 34% of the world's marine fish stocks as overfished.
Stocks of different species can boom and bust in linked ways: as Atlantic blue marlin catches fell in the 1960s, sailfish catches rose.
Fish stock sustainability is tracked under Sustainable Development Goal 14 by indicator 14.4.1.

definition.text: A straddling stock ranges both inside a country's exclusive economic zone and on the high seas; a transboundary stock ranges across the zones of at least two countries.

facts.text: Responsibility for them must be worked out among neighbouring states, usually through an intergovernmental regional organisation.
Straddling stocks are usually mobile open-water species such as herring and mackerel rather than bottom-dwelling ones.

definition.text: Fisheries monitoring, control and surveillance (MCS) widens the enforcement of national fishing rules into support for fisheries management as a whole.

facts.text: Monitoring measures fishing effort and yields; control is the rules under which fishing may happen; surveillance is the observation needed to keep fishers complying.
Success is measured by compliance, not by the number of arrests.
Tools range from fishers' own logbooks and onboard observers to satellite vessel monitoring systems, patrol vessels and aircraft.

definition.text: A fisheries subsidy is a government action that gives fishers or fish consumers an advantage by topping up their income or lowering their costs.

facts.text: Estimates of global fisheries subsidies range from US$15–35 billion a year.
They include direct payments, price support, tax breaks, low-interest loans and preferential treatment.
Some subsidies threaten fish stocks by encouraging overcapacity and excess fishing effort, while others support conservation.
Subsidies are estimated to leave the fishing industry earning US$ 50 billion less per year than it could.
In 2022 the WTO ordered an end to subsidies for illegal fishing, fishing in international waters and fishing of overfished stocks.
Sustainable Development Goal 14 target 14.6 aims to prohibit subsidies that drive overcapacity and overfishing.

title: Fisheries-induced evolution

definition.text: Fisheries-induced evolution is genetic change in a fished population caused by fishing selectively removing individuals with certain traits.

facts.text: It often leads to earlier maturation, smaller adult size and lower fecundity.
Over 500 years of selecting larger Atlantic cod shifted the species toward earlier maturation at smaller sizes.
Even unselective gear can select: fast-growing, active rainbow trout were 60% more likely to be caught in gill nets.
Reduced genetic diversity is predicted to lower populations' ability to adapt to environmental change.

notes: Dossier Definition line S:fa05950da5a1 is a reference title; definition uses the lead sentence.

title: Fishing down the food web

definition.text: Fishing down the food web is the process in which fisheries, having used up the large predatory fish, turn to ever smaller species and finally to small fish and invertebrates once ignored.

facts.text: Daniel Pauly and colleagues first demonstrated it in a 1998 article in Science.
Over the last 50 years, the abundance of large predators such as cod, swordfish and tuna has dropped 90 percent.
Pauly's Ecopath modelling found the mean trophic level of catches fell by between 0.5 and 1.0 levels over 50 years, globally and in each ocean.
Bigger fish usually sit higher in the food chain and fishing tends to take the bigger fish, so intense fishing leaves small fish dominating catches.
Rising prices for small forage fish and invertebrates can be seen as subsidizing fishing down.
In pristine oceans, large predator biomass was 10 to 100 times greater than today.

contested_note: FAO scientists argued Pauly's team misread the catch statistics, and later studies attribute falling catch trophic levels to added low-level fisheries or climate-driven swings rather than predator collapse, finding it not a global phenomenon.

title: Marine Trophic Index
article: Fishing down the food web#Marine Trophic Index

definition.text: The Marine Trophic Index is the average trophic level of a fishery's catch, used as a gauge of marine ecosystem health.

facts.text: In 2000 the Convention on Biological Diversity chose it as one of eight indicators of ecosystem health and asked members to report changes.
A falling index generally means large predators are being depleted and more small forage fish are caught; a steady or rising one signals a stable or improving fishery.
Lucrative crustacean and mollusc fisheries sit at low trophic levels and so pull the index down.

title: Farming up the food web
article: Fishing down the food web#Farming up the web

definition.text: Farming up the food web is the rise in the average trophic level of farmed fish while that of wild catches falls.

facts.text: Mediterranean bluefin tuna farming grew from almost zero in 1986 to 30,000 tonnes by 2005, but it only fattens juveniles caught from the wild.
Feeding high-level fish takes fishmeal from sardines and anchovies people could eat directly, so such farming is a net consumer of fish.

definition.text: Illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing covers fishing without permission or against the law, fishing that is not or wrongly reported, and fishing where no conservation rules apply.

facts.text: It is thought to occur in most fisheries and to make up as much as 30% of catches in some important ones.
It costs the global economy between $10 billion and $23 billion a year, among the most profitable natural resource crimes.
Its environmental harms include biodiversity loss and habitat damage from illegal methods, overfishing and bycatch.
Illegal and unreported fishing arise mainly from failure to enforce existing laws, often rooted in poor national governance.
Mandatory certification and catch documentation are increasingly used to keep IUU products out of markets.
Weak enforcement of fishing rights in artisanal fisheries leads to free-riding and illegal fishing.

conflicts.text: Other studies put annual global losses from IUU fishing at between $25 and $50 billion.
conflicts.note: Different studies; differs from the $10-23 billion estimate.

title: Fisheries crime
article: Illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing#Fisheries crime

definition.text: Fisheries crime is a wider idea than IUU fishing that takes in all criminal activity along the fishing sector's value chain.

facts.text: IUU fishing is closely tied to other organized crimes such as human and drug trafficking, corruption and document fraud.
Human trafficking for forced labour on IUU fishing operations is an increasingly serious issue.

title: International Convention for the Regulation of Whaling
article: International Convention for the Regulation of Whaling

definition.text: The International Convention for the Regulation of Whaling is an international agreement to conserve whale stocks and so allow the whaling industry to develop in an orderly way.

facts.text: It was signed by 15 countries in Washington on 3 December 1946 in response to the overexploitation of whales after World War I.
Its International Whaling Commission meets yearly and sets binding catch limits, methods and protected areas.
It moved whaling from open hunting to highly restricted hunting, though Japan withdrew in 2019 to resume commercial whaling.

contested_note: Members disagree on whether the convention covers only great whales or all cetaceans.

title: Optimum sustainable yield

definition.text: Optimum sustainable yield is the level of fishing effort that maximizes the gap between total revenue and total cost, the resource's economic profit or rent.

facts.text: At this effort level, marginal revenue equals marginal cost.
It usually means less fishing effort than maximum sustainable yield.
In environmental science it is the largest economic yield a renewable resource can give over a long period without weakening the population's or ecosystem's ability to keep supplying it.
Knowing mortality rates helps managers set harvest limits at maximum or optimum sustainable yield.

notes: Definition overlaps heavily with part90 'Maximum economic yield'; the merge pass may fold them.

definition.text: Population dynamics of fisheries is the study of how a fished population grows and shrinks over time through births, deaths and migration.

facts.text: Fisheries scientists use it to work out sustainable yields and optimal harvesting rates.
Its classic model is Verhulst's 1838 logistic equation, in which growth slows as numbers approach the carrying capacity K.
Under logistic growth, maximum sustainable yield sits at exactly half the carrying capacity, where population growth is fastest.
Schaefer's catch equation makes the catch proportional to fishing effort times stock biomass times a catchability parameter.
The Baranov catch equation of 1918 is perhaps the most used equation in fisheries modelling.
The first principle of population dynamics is widely held to be Malthus's exponential law.

definition.text: Recruitment is the number of new young fish entering a population in a given year, usually counted from the age at which they can be caught in nets.

facts.text: Fish populations can swing by orders of magnitude over time, and five to 10-fold variations in abundance are usual.
Swings in reproductive and recruitment success appear to be prime drivers of these fluctuations.
Yearly recruitment often seems random and often relates poorly to adult stock levels and fishing effort.

title: Virtual population analysis
article: Population dynamics of fisheries#Virtual population analysis

definition.text: Virtual population analysis is a fisheries technique that reconstructs past numbers of fish at each age from the yearly deaths in each cohort.

facts.text: Deaths are split into fishery catch and natural mortality.
It is 'virtual' because population size is never measured directly but back-calculated from observed catches and an assumed natural death rate.

definition.text: Fishing effort is a measure of the human work put into catching fish, ideally roughly proportional to the amount caught.

facts.text: A trawl fleet's effort may be measured as engine power times days at sea (kW × days).
A gill-net fishery's effort may be measured as net length times soak time.

definition.text: The von Bertalanffy growth model, published in 1934, describes how fast individual fish grow in length toward a maximum length.

facts.text: In its simplest form, growth in length is proportional to the gap between current length and the ultimate length L∞.
Pauly's method estimates natural mortality from von Bertalanffy growth parameters and temperature.

definition.text: Recreational fishing, also called sport or game fishing, is fishing for leisure, exercise or competition rather than for profit or survival.

facts.text: Its most common form is angling with rod, reel, line, hooks and bait.
It is a multibillion-dollar industry: in the United States in 2014, about 11 million saltwater anglers generated $58 billion in sales impacts.
Governments set licences and rules on lures, bait and hooks to keep it sustainable, and many anglers voluntarily practise catch and release.
Policy makers have largely ignored the sector, though a framework now exists to give it the attention commercial fisheries get.
Stocking non-native fish for sport has caused impacts on aquatic life and drives homogenization of freshwater fish communities.
The earliest English essay on recreational fishing appeared in 1496, and Izaak Walton wrote The Compleat Angler in 1653.

definition.text: A regional fishery body is an international organization set up under a fishery agreement for countries to cooperate on conserving and sustainably using marine living resources.

facts.text: Advisory bodies issue only non-binding, science-led recommendations, while regional fishery management organisations (RFMOs) are more political but their decisions bind members.
RFMOs manage fish stocks in a region or highly migratory species, using catch limits, technical measures, area or season closures, and monitoring.
Members include coastal states and distant-water fishing nations whose fleets travel to the stock.
The main treaty for RFMOs is the 1995 UN Fish Stocks Agreement, which gives access to the fishery only to members or states that follow the organisation's rules.
The International Pacific Halibut Commission of 1924 is seen as an early RFMO.
Some RFMOs focus on particular species such as tuna, while others cover all living marine resources in a region.

definition.text: The Ricker model is a classic population model that predicts the number of individuals in the next generation from the number in the current one.

facts.text: Bill Ricker introduced it in 1954 for stock and recruitment in fisheries, and it can predict how many fish a fishery will hold.
Its parameters are an intrinsic growth rate r and a carrying capacity k.
Unlike the logistic map, its carrying capacity is not a hard ceiling but only sets the overall scale of the population.
It and the Beverton–Holt model are both special cases of the Hassell model.

definition.text: A shifting baseline is when a system is judged against a reference point that itself already reflects large, forgotten changes from an earlier state.

facts.text: Daniel Pauly applied it to fisheries, where experts judged badly depleted fisheries against their state at the start of their own careers rather than the untouched state.
As each generation redefines what is 'natural', large long-term declines become hidden.
The idea first arose in Ian McHarg's 1969 book Design With Nature.
Most modern stock assessments account for historical fishing by including past catches or reconstructing earlier depletion.
Ongoing human-driven change such as climate change creates a shifting baseline that complicates restoring ecosystems to a past reference state.

definition.text: A stock assessment gathers biological and fishery data to give fisheries managers the information they use to regulate a fish stock.

facts.text: Biological data include age structure, fecundity, natural and fishing mortality, growth and an estimate of total population or biomass.
Data come from the fishery itself, such as recorded landings, and from independent surveys using trawls, seines or acoustic and video methods.
Managers use it to predict how stocks will respond to different fishing pressures, aiming to cut overfishing and rebuild overfished stocks.
Common models are surplus production models, which need the least data, statistical age- or length-structured models, and virtual population analysis.
A stock is 'overfished' when its biomass is below what supports maximum sustainable yield; 'overfishing' describes too high a rate of removal.
Modern methods statistically integrate several information sources to estimate management quantities and their uncertainty.

definition.text: Biological reference points are benchmarks produced by stock assessments against which fishing regulations are set.

facts.text: A ratio of current fishing mortality to the mortality giving maximum sustainable yield above one means overfishing is happening.
When fishing mortality exceeds its limit or spawning stock falls below its minimum threshold, the fishery is shut down.
Biomass at maximum sustainable yield is typically around 40-50% of unfished biomass; Australia often targets a more cautious 60%.
Maximum sustainable yield considers only fish biology, while optimum yield also considers the economics of the harvest.

definition.text: Sustainable seafood is fish and shellfish caught or farmed in ways that protect the long-term health of the species, the oceans and the communities that depend on fishing.

facts.text: It comes from sources that can keep up or increase production in future without harming the ecosystems it is taken from.
The sustainable seafood movement began in the 1990s, driven by ecolabels and awareness campaigns that let consumers make informed choices.
Research suggests fisheries can recover or stabilize when responsible management and regulation are in place.
Seasonal fishing limits let fish spawn and replenish, protecting vulnerable life stages.
Modified catfish traps cut turtle bycatch by 84% with no drop in catfish catches.
Certified production of wild seafood has passed 10% of the global share.

title: Seafood ecolabelling

definition.text: Seafood ecolabelling has an independent third party check a fishery's or farm's production against environmental standards, licensing a label for products that pass.

facts.text: The label tells consumers the product was produced sustainably and can bring producers a financial benefit.
The Marine Stewardship Council launched the first seafood certification program in 1996.
MSC certification requires healthy fish stocks, minimal ecosystem impact and effective management.

contested_note: Critics say the MSC has certified troubled or data-poor fisheries; one study found 31% of MSC-certified stocks were overfished.
notes: Contested note draws on S:3dd7555631a7 and S:bc049223968d.

definition.text: Seafood guides tell shoppers which species are fine to eat and which to avoid, based on their environmental impact.

facts.text: Many use three traffic-light categories: red, yellow and green.
Rankings reflect how a species copes with fishing pressure, its abundance, gear impact, bycatch and management.
They let consumers 'vote with their wallets'.

title: Annual sustainable yield
article: Sustainable yield in fisheries#Annual Sustainable Yield

definition.text: Annual sustainable yield is the biomass that can be harvested from a fish population each year without causing it to decline.

facts.text: It is adjusted from year to year according to population levels and how previous seasons went.
Because real carrying capacity fluctuates, maximum sustainable yield may vary yearly, which annual sustainable yields try to account for.

definition.text: Wild fisheries, also called capture fisheries, are natural waters holding free-ranging fish or shellfish populations that are caught for commercial value.

facts.text: They can be marine or freshwater and depend heavily on the carrying capacity of the local ecosystem.
Although fish farming is growing, most fish people eat still comes from wild fisheries, humanity's only significant wild food source.
Significant wild fisheries have collapsed or are close to collapse because of overfishing and pollution.
Global wild fisheries are believed to have peaked and begun to decline.
Upwellings bring nutrients that feed plankton-eating forage fish, which draw larger predators; the Humboldt Current supports a significant share of the world catch.
Threats include pollution, eutrophication and ocean acidification, which may weaken shellfish shells and corals.

definition.text: Trawling is an industrial fishing method that drags a net, called a trawl, through the water behind one or more boats.

facts.text: It is the chief method used to harvest fish commercially.
Its environmental problems are lack of selectivity and physical damage to the seabed.

definition.text: Ghost nets are fishing nets left or lost in the ocean that go on entangling fish, turtles, seabirds and other sea life.

facts.text: Trapped animals suffer starvation, injury, infection and suffocation.

definition.text: Marine conservation is the protection of ocean and sea ecosystems through planned management so that marine resources are not over-exploited.

facts.text: It aims to limit human damage to marine ecosystems, restore damaged ones and preserve vulnerable species.
It draws on marine biology, ecology, oceanography and fisheries science, together with economics, maritime law and policy.
Its tools include marine protected areas with seasonal or permanent closures and zoning, sustainable fisheries, and fishing quotas.
Overfishing is one of the main causes of declining ocean wildlife; FAO reported sustainable stocks fell from 90% in 1974 to 65.8% in 2017.
Researchers suggest integrating customary management into marine conservation, though past attempts to combine the two have often failed.
Baleen whales were nearing extinction when the IWC's global ban on commercial whaling took effect in 1986.

title: Plant genetic resources

definition.text: Plant genetic resources are the variety within plants, built up by human and natural selection over millennia, that can be used for food and agriculture now or in future.

facts.text: Farmers first used them more than 10,000 years ago, selecting from wild plants to develop crops.
They are conserved on farms, ex situ in gene banks, or in situ in the wild, where crop wild relatives supply variation for breeding.
Only about 120 crop species provide around 90% of food needs, and maize, wheat, rice and potatoes supply about 60% of dietary energy.
They were treated as the common heritage of mankind until the Convention on Biological Diversity gave countries sovereignty over them.

contested_note: It is disputed whether genetic data separated from the organism fall under international access and benefit-sharing rules.

title: International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture
article: International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture

definition.text: The International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture, or Plant Treaty, aims to secure food security by conserving, exchanging and sustainably using crop genetic resources and sharing their benefits fairly.

facts.text: The FAO adopted it in November 2001 and it came into force in 2004.
Its Multilateral System gives free access to 64 of the world's most important crops for research, breeding and training.
Exchanges use a mandatory Standard Material Transfer Agreement, allowing 8500 transfers every week.
It recognises farmers' rights, though critics argue these are weakly and unevenly realised.

notes: Navbox page placed in the fisheries dossier; belongs with genetic resources or biodiversity policy, not fisheries.

title: Journal of Political Ecology

definition.text: The Journal of Political Ecology is a peer-reviewed open access journal covering political ecology.

facts.text: It studies links between political economy and human impact on the environment, especially unequal access to resources.
Fishing and marine issues are among its four main research areas.

notes: A journal attached to fisheries by the concept graph; at most a summary entry under political ecology, not a fisheries concept.

definition.text: Maximum economic yield (MEY) is the level of catch that gives society the largest net economic benefit, or profit, from a fishery.

facts.text: Like optimum sustainable yield, it is a harvest rate below maximum sustainable yield.
At MEY the resource rent is at its maximum.
In bioeconomic terms, a fishery is overfished when catches exceed MEY.
A profit-maximising owner fishes until marginal revenue equals marginal cost, the condition the Gordon-Schaefer model uses.

definition.text: Surplus production models are the simplest of the three common kinds of fish stock assessment model, needing the least data.

facts.text: Schaefer's version, based on Verhulst's logistic growth, uses the catch equation H = qEX, linking catch to fishing effort and stock biomass.
Setting catch equal to natural growth gives an equilibrium catch for each long-run level of fishing effort.
These models, which estimate MSY directly, made MSY popular in the 1950s.

definition.text: Fishing effort is the amount of human work put into catching fish; excess effort and overcapacity in fishing fleets threaten the sustainability of fish stocks.

facts.text: A good effort measure is roughly proportional to the catch, for example a trawl fleet's engine power times days at sea (kW × days).
Global landings peaked in the late 1980s and are declining despite rising fishing effort.
Some fisheries subsidies encourage overcapacity and excess effort; WTO members agreed to ban certain such subsidies.
Schaefer assumed that in an unregulated fishery effort rises until no more profit can be made.

definition.text: Optimal harvesting theory uses optimisation methods from economics and operations research to choose the best rate and timing of harvest, and is widely used in fisheries.

facts.text: Population dynamics is the basis for working out optimal harvesting rates.
Economically, the aim is to maximise the present value of all future profits from the resource.
If density dependence acts only on larvae, the optimum is to harvest a single most valuable life stage at MSY.
Faustmann's formula applies the same logic to forests, giving the best harvest age from growth, timber prices and a discount rate.

definition.text: A total allowable catch system caps the catch of a whole fishery: fishers may fish when and how they like until the quota is met, then fishing stops until the next season.

facts.text: A TAC does not remove the underlying competition among fishers for the fish.
TACs often produce overcapitalization of the industry and races between boat crews to land fish before the quota runs out.
In the Alaskan halibut fishery the race became so extreme that the season shrank to a single 24-hour dash, and perishable fish were landed in a clump.
The EU Common Fisheries Policy sets TACs per species and ICES area, yearly or two-yearly, and gives each country a quota from its traditional percentage share.

sources.title: 6.3: Case Study- Marine Fisheries - Engineering LibreTexts (Environmental and Resource Economics (Cabezas))

contested_note: Commentators disagree on whether the policy harmed stocks or merely failed to reverse a decline that predated it.
title: Common Fisheries Policy

definition.text: The Common Fisheries Policy is the European Union's fisheries policy: it sets catch quotas, gives member states access to one another's exclusive economic zones and manages sustainable fishing in the EU's zone.

facts.text: Member states may implement the common principles through licences, limited entry or individual fishing quota, and regulations cover gear and closed areas.
Enforcement is left to member states, with a community inspection service checking them.
The 2013 reform, in force from 1 January 2014, was meant to protect endangered stocks and end discards, with maximum sustainable yield to apply from 2015.
Critics say per-species quotas force fish to be thrown overboard dead, and that its centralised top-down command-and-control approach should give way to participatory governance.
A 2010 study traced stock depletion to mismanagement long before the policy, with British catch rates down 94% over 118 years.
